_note: Shared building blocks for the path planner. CURATED / DEMO: check links and wording before real use.

preferred.label: A degree is the usual route

flexible.label: A degree helps, but skills matter more

communication.label: Communicating clearly
communication.how: Present in seminars, give a talk to a society, and write one clear page a week. Ask for feedback each time.
communication.proof: A recorded presentation or a society talk you gave.

teamwork.label: Teamwork
teamwork.how: Choose group projects and committee roles. Be the person who finishes the boring bit and helps the quietest voice be heard.
teamwork.proof: A group project outcome you can describe in numbers: what the team delivered and your part.

leadership.label: Leadership
leadership.how: Run something small: a society event, a study group, a fundraiser. Move from helper to organiser by year 2.
leadership.proof: An event or project you led, with how many people took part.

resilience.label: Resilience
resilience.how: Enter competitions you might lose, apply for roles you might not get, and note what you changed each time.
resilience.proof: A 'tried, failed, changed, then succeeded' story.

commercial.label: Commercial awareness
commercial.how: Read one business or industry news source daily. Join a society that discusses real companies. Ask: who pays, who gains, what could go wrong?
commercial.proof: A one-page opinion on a real company or sector, written for a society or LinkedIn.

problem_solving.label: Problem solving
problem_solving.how: Take on open-ended projects, not only problem sets. Write down your reasoning, not just the answer.
problem_solving.proof: A project where you found the problem yourself and explain how you solved it.

empathy.label: Empathy and listening
empathy.how: Volunteer with real people: befriending, helplines, mentoring. Practise summarising what someone said before you answer.
empathy.proof: Regular volunteering hours, and what you learned from the people you supported.

initiative.label: Initiative
initiative.how: Start something that did not exist: a club, a small business, a blog, a tool. Small and real beats big and imagined.
initiative.proof: A link to something you built or started, and who used it.

organisation.label: Organisation and reliability
organisation.how: Keep a weekly plan, hit deadlines, and take a role (treasurer, secretary) where others rely on you.
organisation.proof: A role where you managed money, bookings or deadlines for a group.

digital.label: Digital fluency
digital.how: Learn the tools of your field and one AI assistant well, and learn to check what it tells you. Keep notes on what it got wrong.
digital.proof: A project showing you used modern tools, with what you checked and corrected.

alumni.why: People two to ten years ahead of you are the best source of honest information: what the job is really like, what they would do differently, and what got them hired. Most are glad to help if you ask well.
find: Use your university's alumni network or careers service mentoring scheme if it has one.
On LinkedIn, open your university's page, choose Alumni, and filter by what they studied, where they work and what they do.
Ask your tutors, society committee and older students who they know, and ask for introductions.
Look for alumni who spoke at society events, or who are listed as mentors on your students' union or careers pages.
tips: Ask for 15 minutes, not a job.
Do five minutes of homework on them first, and mention one specific thing.
Prepare three questions, send a short thank-you the same day, and tell them what you did with their advice.
Aim for a mix: someone recent, someone mid-career, and someone who changed direction.
alumni.template:
Hello {their_name},

I'm thinking about studying {degree} at {uni}, and I'm interested in a career in {field}. I saw that you studied there and now work in this area, and I'd really value 15 minutes of your time to hear how you got there.

I'd love to ask: {question}

Thank you for considering it, and no problem at all if you're too busy.

Best wishes,
[Your name]
questions: What does a normal week really look like in your job?
What did you do at university that mattered most when you were hired?
What would you do differently if you were starting again?
